                     )

## 2. Regression Models

<br>

R has a standard formula syntax:

<br>

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

y ~ x1 + x2 + x3*x4 + log(x5)
```

## Key Differences

- No class statement - categorical variables must be coded as factors!

- Model output is an object (classic R!)

- You extract results with functions

## Logistic Regression Example

Generalized linear models can be run in R using `glm()` and then specificying the appropriate family.

<br>

Below is an example for a logistic regression using our data:

<br>

```{r}
#| echo: true

model <- glm(OEGest_R3.fact ~ HYPE.recode + DIAB.recode, # model formula
             data = births20to24.final, # model data
             family = binomial(link = "logit")) # model family - here for logistic reg

```

## Logistic Regression Example - Output Structure

Model class type is glm:

<br>

```{r}
#| echo: true

class(model)

```

## Logistic Regression Example - Output Structure

And information is stored in this structure, which tells us how to extract the output:

<br>

```{r}
#| echo: true


str(model)
```

## Logistic Regression Example - Extracting Output

<br>

General summary of model output:

```{r}
#| echo: true

model

```

## Logistic Regression Example - Extracting Output

To obtain the OR and 95% CI, we can exponentiate the coefficients and 95% CI:

<br>

```{r}
#| echo: true

exp(model$coefficients) # exponentiated to obtain OR!
exp(confint(model)) # obtain the 95% CI

```

## 3. Complex Survey Data  

In other stats programs, the survey design is baked into the procedure.

In R, we have to create a survey design object first, then pass that to any summary/modeling functions.

```{r}
#| echo: true 
#| eval: false  

library(survey) # Classic survey package for R  

new.survey.object <- svydesign(   
                        ids = ~psu, #ids - primary sampling unit variable 
                        strata = ~strata, # sampling strata - set to NULL if N/A
                        weights = ~weight, # sampling weight   
                        nest = TRUE # true if PSUs are nested within strata
                      )
```

## Create survey design object - NSCH

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| messages: false

library(survey)

# Create survey object
design_nsch24 <- svydesign(
                    ids = ~HHID, # household id
                    strata = ~STRATUM, # sampling strata variable
                    weights = ~FWC, # weight variable
                    data = nsch2024, # data with CLEANED variables!
                    nest = TRUE # nested design
)

# View class type
class(design_nsch24)
```

## Survey functions: `svymean()` + `svyciprop()`

`svymean()` will show the percentages of each group:

```{r}
#| echo: true

svymean(~ADHD.fact, # variable
        design_nsch24, # design object
        na.rm = TRUE) # necessary if need to remove any missing values
```

<br>

`svyciprop()` for showing the prevalence of a binary indicator:

```{r}
#| echo: true

svyciprop(~ADHD.fact, # variable
           design_nsch24) # design object
```

## Survey functions: `svytable()`

`svytable()` for showing weighted cross-tabs:

```{r}
#| echo: true

# Weighted cross-tab (counts)
tab <- svytable(~ADHD.fact + ANXIETY.fact,
         design_nsch24)

tab

# Weighted Row Proportions
prop.table(tab, margin = 1) # within ADHD.fact

# Weighted Column Proportions
prop.table(tab, margin = 2) # within ANXIETY.fact

```

## Survey functions: `subset()` + `svyglm()`

`subset()` can be used to subset your design object to certain conditions, while `svyglm()` can be used for survey-weighted glms:

```{r}
#| echo: true

# Subset to insured
design_nsch24.insure <- subset(design_nsch24, CURRINS == 1)

# Logistic regression of ADHD.fact on ANXIETY.fact
model.wt <- svyglm(
            ADHD.fact ~ ANXIETY.fact, # formula
            design = design_nsch24.insure,
            family = quasibinomial()
)

# View and extract the model object like you would with a regular glm()!
summary(model.wt)

exp(model.wt$coefficients)
exp(confint(model.wt))
```

<br>

::: callout-tip
`svycontrast()` can be used for custom contrast statements!
:::

## 4. Spatial Analysis

R is a phenomenal tool for mapping and spatial analysis!

- Data manipulation: read/write ESRI shapefiles, prepare R spatial objects (`sf`, `sp`), geocoding\*

- Data visualization: choropleth, points, density

- Spatial statistics: hotspots, point pattern analysis, modeling, bayesian methods

## Loading spatial data into R

`sf` package: loading shapefile data as a spatial `sf` class:

```{r}
#| echo: true 

# sf package
library(sf)

# load ESRI shapefile (.shp) into R as an sf class
usvi.sf <- sf::read_sf("r fundamentals pngs/2020 Subdistrict/tl_2020_78_cousub.shp")

# check class
class(usvi.sf)
```

## Basic choropleth mapping

`tmap`: basic mapping of polygons and points

```{r}
#| echo: true 
#| warning: false 

# tmap package
library(tmap)

# basic choropleth map
tm_shape(usvi.sf) + # sf object
  tm_polygons("ALAND") # polygon of "variable"
  

```

## Basic choropleth mapping cont.

Like we did with our report figures, we can customize further:

```{r}
#| echo: true 
#| warning: false 
#| eval: false

# basic choropleth map w/ customization
usvi.sf %>% # sf object
  filter(NAMELSAD != "Island subdivision not defined") %>% # removing the empty geometry
  tm_shape() + # specify tmap object
  tm_polygons("ALAND", # polygon of "variable"
              palette = "Purples", # change color
              n = 6, # specify number breaks
              border.col = "darkgrey" # add a border
              ) +  
  tm_layout(main.title = "My Map", #  add a map title
            main.title.position = c("center"),
            frame = FALSE # remove border of map
            ) 

```

## Basic choropleth mapping cont.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false 

# basic choropleth map w/ customization
usvi.sf %>% # sf object
  filter(NAMELSAD != "Island subdivision not defined") %>% # removing the empty geometry
  tm_shape() + # specify tmap object
  tm_polygons("ALAND", # polygon of "variable"
              palette = "Purples", # change color
              n = 6, # specify number breaks
              border.col = "darkgrey" # add a border
              ) +  
  tm_layout(main.title = "My Map", #  add a map title
            main.title.position = c("center"),
            frame = FALSE # remove border of map
            ) 
```
